clinicalPearls: SPG29 is a rare autosomal dominant, complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia linked to chromosome 1p31.1-p21.1, with no gene yet identified.
It was described in a single family and is characterised by childhood or adolescent onset spastic paraparesis with additional systemic features.
The hallmark associated feature is high-frequency sensorineural hearing impairment accompanying the spastic gait.
Persistent vomiting due to a hiatus hernia with gastro-oesophageal reflux is a distinctive part of the phenotype.
A history of neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice) has been noted in affected family members.
The combination of pyramidal signs, deafness and upper gastrointestinal symptoms distinguishes SPG29 from pure dominant subtypes such as SPG4.
No molecular test for the locus exists, so diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion; testable dominant HSP genes should be screened first.
Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary — antispasticity treatment, audiology support and treatment of reflux and hiatus hernia.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG29 is an autosomal dominant complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped by linkage to chromosome 1p31.1-p21.1 in one family; the causative gene has not been identified and the molecular mechanism is therefore unproven. The spastic paraparesis reflects the usual HSP process of length-dependent corticospinal tract degeneration, while the associated high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, hiatus hernia with persistent vomiting and neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia indicate a pleiotropic gene whose product is expressed well beyond the central motor pathways. The co-occurrence of an auditory phenotype with a structural and functional gastro-oesophageal abnormality suggests the underlying gene participates in developmental or membrane-trafficking processes affecting cochlear, diaphragmatic or oesophageal and neuronal tissues alike, and it is this multisystem combination that defines the subtype.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (SPAST) and other pure dominant HSP subtypes lacking deafness
Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome and other disorders combining spasticity with sensorineural deafness
Mitochondrial disorders presenting with spasticity, deafness and multisystem features
SPG7 (paraplegin) complicated HSP with additional signs
Silver syndrome (SPG17/BSCL2) and HSP with amyotrophy or neuropathy
Peroxisomal and other metabolic leukodystrophies with combined neurological and systemic features
additionalInvestigations: Pure-tone audiometry and formal audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
Genetic testing of testable dominant HSP genes and broad exome analysis
MRI brain and spine to exclude structural and complicating lesions
Upper gastrointestinal evaluation and imaging for hiatus hernia and reflux
Nerve conduction studies to assess for associated neuropathy
Metabolic and mitochondrial screening where a multisystem disorder is suspected
redFlags: Progressive hearing loss or feeding and vomiting problems in a child that are being overlooked while attention is on the gait
Recurrent vomiting causing aspiration or failure to thrive, requiring urgent gastrointestinal assessment
Rapid neurological deterioration or new bulbar signs atypical for HSP
Encephalopathy, lactic acidosis or multisystem crisis suggesting a mitochondrial disorder
reference.prognosis: SPG29 is slowly progressive, and the neurological disability is generally mild to moderate over time. Prognosis is also shaped by the associated hearing loss and by control of reflux and vomiting, with life expectancy usually preserved.
pitfalls: Treating the spastic paraparesis in isolation and missing the associated deafness and gastro-oesophageal features that define the syndrome
Expecting a confirmatory gene test, when SPG29 is defined only by linkage in a single family
Attributing the vomiting to a primary gastrointestinal illness rather than recognising it as part of the syndrome
Mistaking the picture for an acquired or mitochondrial multisystem disorder without adequate work-up
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical genetics reviews
Neurogenetics reference databases (gene and locus catalogues)
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and walking aids to maintain gait
Audiological management of the high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with hearing aids and hearing-preservation follow-up
Treat gastro-oesophageal reflux with a proton-pump inhibitor and manage the hiatus hernia, including fundoplication assessment for persistent vomiting
Nutritional monitoring and support given the persistent vomiting
Genetic counselling and cascade testing for autosomal dominant inheritance
Escalate to gastroenterology, upper-gastrointestinal surgery and audiology as systemic features evolve
